questions.title: Portal hypertension and pulmonary bilharziasis
questions.question: Portal hypertension complicating hepatic bilharziasis can predispose to which of the following?

explanations.A: Correct. Hepatic bilharziasis raises portal pressure, and that portal hypertension opens portosystemic venous shunts. Schistosome ova can then bypass the liver's normal filtering and reach the lungs through those shunts, producing pulmonary bilharziasis. This is why pulmonary involvement is seen specifically in patients with the hepatosplenic (portal-hypertensive) form of the disease, not simply in anyone infected with schistosomes.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Portal hypertension does not cause primary lung carcinoma; the recognised pulmonary complication of hepatic bilharziasis is pulmonary bilharziasis itself, via shunted ova.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Portal hypertension has no specific mechanistic link to pulmonary tuberculosis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pulmonary bilharziasis via portosystemic shunting is a recognised complication of portal hypertension in hepatic bilharziasis.

questions.learning_objective: State that portal hypertension from hepatic bilharziasis can predispose to pulmonary bilharziasis.

questions.title: Commonest site in bilharzial cystitis
questions.question: Which site is most commonly affected in bilharzial cystitis?

explanations.A: Correct. Within the bladder, bilharzial cystitis most commonly affects the trigone, the triangular area between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice. This matches the general pattern of schistosome egg deposition and inflammation being heaviest near the ureteric openings. Recognising the trigone as the classic site helps localise gross and cystoscopic findings correctly.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The bladder dome is not the classic site; the trigone is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The bladder neck alone is not the classic site; involvement is centred on the trigone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The urethra is not the bladder site described by this classic teaching; the trigone is.

questions.learning_objective: State that the bladder trigone is the commonest site affected in bilharzial cystitis.

questions.title: Schistosomiasis liver change
questions.question: Which best describes the hepatic change caused by schistosomiasis?

options.A: Periportal ("pipe-stem") fibrosis, distinct from true cirrhosis

explanations.A: Correct. Hepatic schistosomiasis produces periportal (pipe-stem) fibrosis around portal tracts, a presinusoidal pattern of fibrosis. True cirrhosis is defined by diffuse fibrosis together with nodular regeneration, which the schistosomal pattern lacks — so it is taught specifically as a distinct entity from cirrhosis rather than a form of it. The distinction matters because the two conditions carry different natural histories and monitoring needs.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Schistosomal liver fibrosis does not show the nodular regeneration that defines micronodular cirrhosis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Schistosomal liver fibrosis does not show the nodular regeneration that defines macronodular cirrhosis either.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Schistosomiasis causes fibrosis, specifically periportal fibrosis, not isolated fatty change without fibrosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that hepatic schistosomiasis causes periportal fibrosis, not true cirrhosis.

questions.title: Hypersplenism and hepatic bilharzial fibrosis
questions.question: Hypersplenism is a recognised complication of which condition?

options.A: Hepatic bilharzial fibrosis, via portal-hypertension-driven splenomegaly
options.B: Acute viral hepatitis alone, without portal hypertension
options.D: It is not a recognised complication of any liver disease

explanations.A: Correct. Hepatic bilharzial fibrosis raises portal pressure, which causes splenomegaly; a chronically enlarged spleen can progress to hypersplenism, excess destruction/sequestration of blood cells by the spleen, producing cytopenias. This is why patients with long-standing hepatosplenic bilharziasis are monitored for cytopenias in addition to their liver disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Uncomplicated acute viral hepatitis without portal hypertension does not typically drive hypersplenism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Simple fatty liver, without portal hypertension, is not the classic route to hypersplenism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Hypersplenism is a well-recognised complication of portal-hypertensive liver diseases, including hepatic bilharzial fibrosis.

questions.learning_objective: State that hypersplenism is a complication of hepatic bilharzial fibrosis via portal hypertension.

questions.title: Bilharzial malignancy type
questions.question: Bilharzial malignancy of the bladder is classically which histological type?

explanations.A: Correct. Chronic bilharzial irritation classically drives squamous metaplasia and then squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma — this is a standard exception to the usual expectation that GI/GU-tract malignancies are adenocarcinomas, and is worth memorising specifically because it is tested as an exception. Recognising this changes which histology a clinician expects when screening a bilharzial-endemic population.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Adenocarcinoma is not the classic bilharzial malignancy; squamous cell carcinoma is.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Small cell carcinoma is not the classic bilharzial-associated histology.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bilharzial malignancy is classically epithelial (squamous cell carcinoma), not a sarcoma of mesenchymal origin.

questions.learning_objective: State that bilharzial malignancy is classically squamous cell carcinoma, not adenocarcinoma.

questions.title: Sandy patches: bladder versus colon
questions.question: "Sandy patches" (pale, granular egg-deposit plaques) are more characteristic of which site in bilharziasis?

explanations.A: Correct. "Sandy patches" are a gross feature described more often in urinary bladder bilharziasis than in bilharzial colitis, reflecting the heavier egg burden typically seen in the bladder for this presentation. This site preference is a useful discriminator when the gross specimen alone does not make the organ of origin obvious.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Sandy patches are described more often in the bladder than in the colon, the reverse of this option.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Sandy patches are a bladder/colon mucosal finding, not a classic liver finding.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Sandy patches are not a described feature of pulmonary bilharziasis.

questions.learning_objective: State that sandy patches are more characteristic of the bladder than the colon in bilharziasis.

questions.title: Which bladder metaplasia is precancerous
questions.question: Which bladder urothelial metaplastic change is considered precancerous?

explanations.A: Correct. Cystitis glandularis, particularly its intestinal-type variant, is considered a precancerous lesion of the bladder urothelium, carrying an association with subsequent adenocarcinoma. Cystitis cystica, by contrast, is considered a benign metaplastic change without that same premalignant association.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cystitis cystica is the one of the pair NOT considered precancerous.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cystitis glandularis specifically is flagged as precancerous.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The two related-sounding lesions do not carry equal cancer risk; only cystitis glandularis is precancerous.

questions.learning_objective: State that cystitis glandularis is considered a precancerous lesion, unlike cystitis cystica.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Infectious and parasitic pathology

questions.title: Cystitis cystica and cancer risk
questions.question: Cystitis cystica is generally considered:

options.A: A benign metaplastic change, not precancerous

explanations.A: Correct. Cystitis cystica is a benign metaplastic change of the bladder urothelium (a cystic variant of von Brunn's nests), taught without the premalignant association that cystitis glandularis carries. Confusing the two related-sounding "cystitis X" terms and assuming both carry the same cancer risk is a common exam trap.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Cystitis glandularis, not cystitis cystica, is the precancerous member of this pair.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cystitis cystica is a benign metaplastic change, not an invasive malignancy.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Cystitis cystica is an acquired metaplastic change, not a congenital anomaly.

questions.learning_objective: State that cystitis cystica is not considered a precancerous lesion, unlike cystitis glandularis.

questions.title: Lepromatous leprosy and T-cell immunity
questions.question: Which form of leprosy is characterised by lack of T-cell mediated immunity against M. leprae?

options.D: Neither; leprosy has no immune-mediated spectrum

explanations.A: Correct. Lepromatous leprosy is the pole of the disease spectrum defined by poor/absent T-cell mediated immunity against M. leprae, which permits widespread bacillary proliferation and disseminated disease. This is the opposite immunological state from tuberculoid leprosy, which has strong T-cell immunity that limits the disease.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tuberculoid leprosy is the pole WITH strong T-cell immunity, not the pole that lacks it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The two poles have opposite, not equal, T-cell immune responses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Leprosy's clinical spectrum is specifically defined by the host's cell-mediated immune response.

questions.learning_objective: State that lepromatous leprosy is characterised by lack of T-cell mediated immunity.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Infectious and parasitic pathology

questions.title: Lepromin test in lepromatous leprosy
questions.question: The lepromin skin test is characteristically which result in lepromatous leprosy?

explanations.A: Correct. The lepromin skin test reflects cell-mediated immunity against M. leprae, which is absent in lepromatous leprosy — so the test is negative there. It is tuberculoid leprosy, with its strong T-cell response, that gives a strongly positive lepromin test. Swapping which pole gets a positive versus negative result is a classic exam trap.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A strongly positive lepromin test is characteristic of tuberculoid, not lepromatous, leprosy.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lepromin test gives a fairly consistent negative result in lepromatous leprosy, not an equivocal one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lepromin test is specifically used to help place a leprosy patient on the immunological spectrum.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lepromin test is negative, not positive, in lepromatous leprosy.

questions.title: Which syphilis stage shows the chancre
questions.question: The chancre is the characteristic lesion of which stage of syphilis?

explanations.A: Correct. The chancre — a painless, firm, indurated lesion at the inoculation site — is specifically the defining lesion of primary syphilis. Secondary syphilis instead classically presents with a diffuse maculopapular rash and other systemic features, after the chancre has healed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secondary syphilis presents with a diffuse rash and systemic features, not the chancre.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tertiary syphilis presents with gummas and cardiovascular/neurological complications, not the chancre.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The chancre is a feature of acquired primary syphilis, not specifically congenital syphilis.

questions.learning_objective: State that the chancre is a primary-, not secondary-, syphilis lesion.

questions.title: Syphilitic aortic aneurysm site
questions.question: Syphilitic aortitis classically produces aneurysm at which site?

options.A: The ascending aorta and aortic arch

explanations.A: Correct. Tertiary syphilis causes an obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum, classically damaging the ascending aorta and aortic arch and predisposing to aneurysm there — a thoracic-aorta disease pattern, the opposite site emphasis from the abdominal-aorta aneurysms typically caused by atherosclerosis. Recognising this site preference helps distinguish a syphilitic aneurysm from the far more common atherosclerotic abdominal aortic aneurysm.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The abdominal aorta is the classic site for atherosclerotic aneurysm, not syphilitic aortitis.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Syphilitic aortitis targets the aorta itself, not the pulmonary artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The renal arteries are not the classic site of syphilitic aortitis.

questions.learning_objective: State that syphilitic aortitis classically affects the ascending aorta and aortic arch.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Infectious and parasitic pathology

questions.title: Timeline of tertiary syphilis
questions.question: Tertiary syphilis typically develops how long after the initial infection?

options.D: It develops simultaneously with the primary chancre

explanations.A: Correct. Tertiary syphilis follows years after the initial infection, once the untreated disease has passed through its latent period — a much longer timeline than the primary-to-secondary transition. This long latency is why untreated syphilis can appear to resolve for years before gummas, cardiovascular disease or neurosyphilis re-emerge.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The 2-12 week interval instead separates primary syphilis (the chancre) from the onset of secondary syphilis, not tertiary disease.
explanations.C: Incorrect. No stage of syphilis develops on a 24-48 hour timescale.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Tertiary disease follows years after, not simultaneously with, the primary chancre.

questions.learning_objective: State that tertiary syphilis occurs years, not weeks, after infection.

questions.title: Syphilitic gummas and their stage
questions.question: Syphilitic gummas are a manifestation of which stage of syphilis?

explanations.A: Correct. Gummas — localised granulomatous lesions with central necrosis — are a classic manifestation of tertiary syphilis, occurring years after the initial infection, alongside cardiovascular complications such as aortitis. Distinguishing a gumma from the lesions of primary (chancre) or secondary (rash) syphilis by its stage and timing is a routinely tested distinction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Primary syphilis presents with the chancre, not a gumma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Secondary syphilis presents with a diffuse rash, not a gumma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Gummas are a manifestation of acquired tertiary syphilis, not specifically congenital disease.

questions.learning_objective: State that syphilitic gummas occur in tertiary syphilis.

questions.title: Syphilitic tongue lesions and cancer risk
questions.question: Syphilitic lesions of the tongue are generally considered:

options.B: Entirely benign, with no malignant potential
options.D: Unrelated to any cancer risk, purely infectious

explanations.A: Correct. Syphilitic glossitis/gummas of the tongue are considered precancerous lesions, carrying an increased risk of subsequent squamous cell carcinoma of the tongue — one of several named precancerous conditions of the oral cavity worth remembering together. Recognising this precancerous status supports closer surveillance of syphilitic tongue lesions rather than dismissing them as purely infectious.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Syphilitic tongue lesions carry a recognised malignant-potential association, not none.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Precancerous" means increased risk, not that the lesion is already malignant at presentation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Syphilitic tongue lesions are specifically flagged for their cancer-risk association, not treated as purely infectious with no such link.

questions.learning_objective: State that syphilitic tongue lesions are precancerous.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Infectious and parasitic pathology

questions.title: Most severe form of leprosy
questions.question: Which form of leprosy is the most severe/disseminated?

options.D: Borderline leprosy is always the most severe form

explanations.A: Correct. Lepromatous leprosy, with its poor T-cell mediated immunity and widespread bacillary dissemination, is the more severe and more infectious form. Tuberculoid (maculoanaesthetic) leprosy has a strong T-cell response that limits the disease to a few well-defined, anaesthetic skin lesions, causing more local tissue damage from that immune reaction but far less overall disease burden.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Tuberculoid leprosy is the milder, more locally contained pole of the disease, not the most severe form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The two poles differ substantially in severity; they are not equally severe.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Borderline leprosy occupies an intermediate position and is not, by definition, always the most severe form.

questions.learning_objective: State that lepromatous, not tuberculoid, leprosy is the more severe form.

questions.title: Is actinomycosis a fungal disease
questions.question: Actinomycosis is caused by an organism best classified as:

explanations.A: Correct. Actinomyces species are filamentous, branching, Gram-positive bacteria, part of normal oral/GI flora, that cause disease when introduced into deeper tissue. The organism's historical association with fungal disease came from its fungus-like microscopic appearance ("ray fungus", sulfur granules), not from any true fungal biology.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Despite the fungus-like branching-filament appearance, Actinomyces is a bacterium, not a fungus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Actinomycosis is caused by a bacterium, not a virus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Actinomycosis is caused by a bacterium, not a protozoan parasite.

questions.learning_objective: State that actinomycosis is bacterial, not fungal, despite its name and morphology.

questions.title: Definition of toxemia
questions.question: Which term names the circulation of toxins in the blood, causing clinical and pathological manifestations?

explanations.A: Correct. Toxemia specifically names the circulation of toxins in the blood — not necessarily live organisms — causing clinical and pathological manifestations, distinct from bacteremia (mere bacterial presence) and septicemia (actively multiplying organisms producing toxins in the blood itself). Recognising toxemia as its own category is what lets these three related words be used precisely rather than interchangeably.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteremia names the mere presence of bacteria in blood, not specifically circulating toxins.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Septicemia names actively multiplying, toxin-producing organisms in blood, a broader/different state than toxemia's toxin-only definition.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyemia names septic emboli seeding distant abscesses, not circulating toxins.

questions.learning_objective: Define toxemia as circulating toxins causing clinical/pathological manifestations.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Infectious and parasitic pathology

questions.title: Bacteremia versus septicemia
questions.question: Circulation of large numbers of virulent, actively multiplying, toxin-producing micro-organisms in the blood is called:

explanations.A: Correct. Septicemia is the more severe state of active organism multiplication and toxin production in the blood itself. Bacteremia, by contrast, is simply the presence of bacteria in the blood, without necessarily any multiplication there. Using "bacteremia" and "septicemia" interchangeably is a common but important error.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bacteremia describes mere bacterial presence, not active multiplication and toxin production — that is septicemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Toxemia describes circulating toxins specifically, not necessarily actively multiplying organisms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Viremia specifically refers to viruses in the blood, not bacteria.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish bacteremia (mere presence) from septicemia (active multiplication and toxin production).

questions.title: Are pyemic abscesses chronic
questions.question: Pyemic abscesses, seeded by septic emboli, are typically:

explanations.A: Correct. Pyemia is seeded by septic emboli — fragments of infected thrombus travelling through the bloodstream and lodging in distant organs. Each lodged embolus forms an acute abscess rapidly at that site, rather than a slow, chronic collection, even if the abscess is only discovered some time after it formed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pyemic abscesses form acutely, not as slow, chronic collections.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pyemic abscesses are infective by definition, seeded by septic (infected) emboli.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pyemic abscesses are acquired, seeded by septic emboli, not congenital.

questions.learning_objective: State that pyemic abscesses, from septic emboli, are acute lesions.

questions.title: Which tissue shows red infarction
questions.question: Which best describes red (haemorrhagic) infarction?

options.A: Occurs in loose tissue with a dual/collateral blood supply, e.g. lung
options.B: Occurs in solid organs with a single end-artery supply, e.g. heart/kidney/spleen
options.C: Occurs only in avascular tissue such as cartilage
options.D: Occurs exclusively following venous, never arterial, occlusion

explanations.A: Correct. Red (haemorrhagic) infarction occurs in loose, spongy tissues with a dual or collateral blood supply, classically the lung, where blood from the second supply (or venous back-flow) re-enters and pools in the necrotic zone, giving the infarct its haemorrhagic, red appearance. This is the reverse pattern from pale infarction, which occurs in solid, single-end-artery-supplied organs such as the heart, kidney and spleen.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This description matches pale (white) infarction, not red infarction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Avascular tissue such as cartilage does not typically infarct in this classic sense at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Infarction can follow arterial occlusion as well as venous occlusion; red infarction is not restricted to venous causes.

questions.learning_objective: State that red infarction occurs in loose, dual-supplied tissue such as the lung.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Definition of edema
questions.question: Which correctly defines edema?

options.A: Increased interstitial fluid, or an excessive body-cavity fluid accumulation
options.B: Decreased interstitial fluid from lymphatic overactivity
options.C: Accumulation of blood, rather than fluid, within tissue spaces
options.D: Accumulation of pus within a confined space

explanations.A: Correct. Edema is defined as increased interstitial fluid or an excessive body-cavity fluid accumulation (an effusion). It is a sign of an underlying imbalance in the Starling forces, not a disease in itself.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Edema is an increase, not a decrease, in interstitial fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Accumulation of blood within tissue is haemorrhage, not edema.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Accumulation of pus within a confined space is an abscess, not edema.

questions.learning_objective: Define edema as excess interstitial fluid or an excessive body-cavity fluid accumulation.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Definition of congestion
questions.question: Which correctly defines congestion?

options.A: Passive dilatation of veins/capillaries from impaired venous drainage
options.B: Active arteriolar dilatation from increased arterial inflow
options.C: Narrowing of arterioles that reduces blood flow
options.D: Complete cessation of blood flow to a tissue

explanations.A: Correct. Congestion is a passive process: veins and capillaries dilate because venous drainage is impaired, so blood backs up in the tissue. This is the opposite mechanism from hyperemia, an active process from increased arterial inflow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes hyperemia, not congestion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Arteriolar narrowing that reduces flow describes ischaemia, not congestion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Complete cessation of blood flow describes infarction's precipitating event, not congestion, which is excess (not absent) blood.

questions.learning_objective: Define congestion as passive vascular dilatation from impaired venous drainage.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Deep leg vein thromboembolus destination
questions.question: A thromboembolus arising in the deep leg veins most commonly lodges where?

explanations.A: Correct. A thromboembolus from the deep leg veins commonly detaches, travels through the venous system and right heart, and lodges in a peripheral branch of the pulmonary artery — a pulmonary embolism. This is the classic pathway from deep vein thrombosis to pulmonary embolism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A venous (leg-vein) embolus cannot reach a coronary artery directly, since it travels through the right heart and lungs, not the systemic arterial circulation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A venous embolus would reach a cerebral artery only via an abnormal right-to-left shunt, not as the typical/expected route.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A leg-vein embolus travels toward the lungs via the inferior vena cava and right heart, not toward the portal vein.

questions.learning_objective: State that a deep-leg-vein thromboembolus commonly lodges in a peripheral pulmonary arterial branch.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Which tissue shows pale infarction
questions.question: Which best describes pale (white/anaemic) infarction?

options.A: Occurs in solid organs with a single end-artery supply, e.g. heart/kidney/spleen
options.B: Occurs in loose, dual-supplied tissue such as the lung
options.C: Is always haemorrhagic in gross appearance

explanations.A: Correct. Pale (white/anaemic) infarction occurs in solid organs supplied by a single end-artery with no effective collateral — classically the heart, kidney and spleen — so no blood can re-enter the dead zone once the single supply is cut, unlike the dual-supplied lung. This is the reverse pattern from red infarction, which occurs in loose, dual-supplied tissues such as the lung.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes red, not pale, infarction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. "Pale" infarction is, by definition, not haemorrhagic in gross appearance — that contradicts its own name.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pale infarction typically follows arterial occlusion of an end-artery-supplied organ.

questions.learning_objective: State that pale infarction occurs in end-artery-supplied solid organs (heart, kidney, spleen).
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Definition of hyperemia
questions.question: Which correctly defines hyperemia?

options.A: An active process from increased arterial blood inflow due to arteriolar dilatation
options.B: A passive process from impaired venous drainage
options.C: Cessation of arterial inflow to a tissue
options.D: Accumulation of fluid within a body cavity

explanations.A: Correct. Hyperemia is an active process: arterioles dilate, increasing arterial inflow and delivering more blood to a tissue — the opposite mechanism from congestion, a passive process from impaired venous drainage. Recognising which mechanism is at work in a given clinical scenario, e.g. early acute inflammation versus chronic right heart failure, depends on telling the two apart.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes congestion, not hyperemia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Hyperemia is increased, not absent, arterial inflow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Fluid accumulation in a body cavity is an effusion (a form of edema), not hyperemia.

questions.learning_objective: Define hyperemia as active vascular dilatation from increased arterial inflow.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Source of most pulmonary emboli
questions.question: What proportion of pulmonary emboli originate from thrombi of the deep leg veins?

options.D: Essentially 0%; most originate from the heart

explanations.A: Correct. Deep leg vein thrombi so dominate as an embolic source that they account for roughly 95% of pulmonary emboli, making deep vein thrombosis the dominant source to screen for whenever a pulmonary embolism is found. This heavy skew toward one source is why DVT prophylaxis is, in practice, pulmonary-embolism-prevention as well.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Deep leg veins account for far more than half of pulmonary emboli, roughly 95%.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 10% understates the dominant role deep leg veins play as an embolic source.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deep leg veins, not the heart, are the overwhelmingly dominant source of pulmonary emboli.

questions.learning_objective: State that about 95% of pulmonary emboli originate from deep leg vein thrombi.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Definition of gangrene
questions.question: Which correctly defines gangrene?

options.A: Necrosis with superadded bacterial putrefaction, classically clostridial, producing gas and toxins
options.C: A reversible form of cell injury

explanations.A: Correct. Gangrene is necrotic tissue with superadded bacterial putrefaction, classically by clostridial organisms, producing gas and toxins — this bacterial-breakdown step is what distinguishes gangrene from plain, sterile necrosis. Recognising this requirement guides whether antimicrobial therapy and surgical debridement are needed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Necrosis without bacterial involvement is plain (sterile) necrosis, not gangrene.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Gangrene, like all necrosis, is irreversible cell death, not a reversible injury.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Programmed cell death without inflammation describes apoptosis, a distinct process from gangrene.

questions.learning_objective: Define gangrene as necrosis with superadded bacterial putrefaction, classically clostridial.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Nutmeg liver appearance
questions.question: Chronic venous congestion of the liver classically produces which gross appearance on the cut surface?

options.A: A mottled "nutmeg" pattern (dark centrilobular zones against pale periportal zones)
options.B: A uniformly pale, greasy cut surface

explanations.A: Correct. Chronic hepatic venous congestion, most often from right-sided heart failure, produces a mottled cut surface — congested, dark-red centrilobular zones alternating with paler periportal zones — resembling a nutmeg seed's cut surface. This gross pattern is a classic autopsy and imaging sign of long-standing right heart failure specifically.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A uniformly pale, greasy cut surface describes fatty change, not chronic venous congestion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Multiple small regenerative nodules describe cirrhosis, a different process from chronic venous congestion.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A diffusely yellow, shrunken liver does not describe the specific mottled nutmeg pattern of chronic congestion.

questions.learning_objective: Identify chronic hepatic venous congestion by its nutmeg-pattern cut surface.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Starling forces count
questions.question: How many primary forces (Starling forces) determine fluid movement across the capillary membrane?

explanations.A: Correct. Capillary hydrostatic pressure, interstitial colloid osmotic pressure, plasma colloid osmotic pressure and interstitial hydrostatic pressure are the four opposing Starling forces that together determine net fluid movement across the capillary wall. An imbalance among any of these four is the shared underlying mechanism behind most clinical causes of edema.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two forces would omit half of the recognised set.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Three forces would still omit one of the recognised four.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Six overstates the recognised count; four is standard.

questions.learning_objective: Name the four Starling forces that determine capillary fluid movement.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Virchow's triad count
questions.question: How many factors make up Virchow's triad?

explanations.A: Correct. Virchow's triad names endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability as the three factors that predispose to thrombosis, any one of which can tip the balance toward thrombus formation. Which factor dominates in a given clinical scenario, e.g. immobility favouring stasis, shapes where and how a thrombus is likely to form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Two factors would omit one of the recognised triad.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Four overstates the recognised count; three is standard.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Five overstates the recognised count considerably; three is standard.

questions.learning_objective: Name Virchow's triad: endothelial injury, abnormal flow, hypercoagulability.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Infarction type in the lung
questions.question: The lung, with its dual bronchial/pulmonary arterial supply, classically shows which type of infarction?

options.B: White (pale) infarction, as in end-artery organs
options.C: No infarction can occur in the lung, due to its dual supply
options.D: Infarction only from venous, never arterial, occlusion

explanations.A: Correct. Because the lung has a dual blood supply, blood from the second source (or venous back-flow) can re-enter the ischaemic zone, giving the infarct a haemorrhagic, red appearance rather than a pale one. This is the reverse pattern from solid, single-end-artery-supplied organs (heart, kidney, spleen), which show pale infarction.
explanations.B: Incorrect. White (pale) infarction is the pattern of end-artery-supplied solid organs, not the dual-supplied lung.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lung can still infarct despite its dual supply; the dual supply changes the infarct's colour (to red), not whether infarction can occur.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pulmonary infarction is not restricted to venous causes; arterial occlusion (e.g. embolism) is a recognised cause too.

questions.learning_objective: State that the lung classically shows red, not white/pale, infarction.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Hemodynamic disorders

questions.title: Definition of dysplasia
questions.question: Which is the correct definition of dysplasia?

options.A: Disordered growth/maturation within one tissue type, with loss of cell uniformity and architectural orientation
options.B: Replacement of one differentiated tissue by another differentiated tissue
options.C: Irreversible, autonomous proliferation of a new clone of cells
options.D: An increase in cell number achieved by cell division

explanations.A: Correct. Dysplasia is disordered growth and maturation within a single tissue type — loss of cell uniformity and architectural orientation — without the tissue converting to a different type. This is distinct from metaplasia, which involves an actual tissue-type change.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes metaplasia's definition, not dysplasia's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes neoplasia, an irreversible autonomous process, distinct from dysplasia, which remains a disordered but not yet autonomous growth pattern.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An increase in cell number by division describes hyperplasia, not dysplasia.

questions.learning_objective: State that dysplasia is disordered growth within one tissue type, not tissue replacement.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Dysplasia is replacement of one differentiated tissue by another", p399

questions.title: Definition of choristoma
questions.question: Which is the correct definition of a choristoma?

options.A: Normal tissue growing in an abnormal site
options.B: Disorganised native tissue growing in its own normal site
options.C: A tumor derived from totipotent cells, containing tissue from more than one germ layer
options.D: A benign tumor of glandular epithelium

explanations.A: Correct. A choristoma is a mass of histologically normal tissue growing in an abnormal (ectopic) location — the opposite of a hamartoma, which is disorganised native tissue in its own normal site. Recognising which of the two applies to a given lesion, right tissue in the wrong place versus disorganised tissue in the right place, is the distinguishing question the exam tests.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes a hamartoma, not a choristoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes a teratoma, a different developmental tumour entirely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes an adenoma, a benign glandular epithelial tumour, not a choristoma.

questions.learning_objective: Define choristoma as normal tissue in an abnormal site.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

questions.title: Staging versus grading
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes tumour staging from grading?

options.A: Grading expresses degree of differentiation; staging expresses extent of spread
options.B: Staging expresses degree of differentiation; grading expresses extent of spread
options.C: Both terms refer only to extent of spread
options.D: Both terms refer only to degree of differentiation

explanations.A: Correct. Grading denotes a tumour's degree of differentiation, and staging denotes its extent of spread — two separate axes for describing a malignant tumour that are commonly swapped in exam distractors. Staging, based on tumour size, nodal involvement and metastasis, generally carries more prognostic weight in clinical decision-making than grading does.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This swaps the two definitions; staging is extent of spread, not differentiation.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Grading specifically addresses differentiation, not extent of spread; the two terms are not synonyms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Staging specifically addresses extent of spread, not differentiation; the two terms are not synonyms.

questions.learning_objective: State that grading (not staging) measures differentiation, and staging (not grading) measures extent of spread.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Staging denotes...differentiation whereas grading...spread", p399

questions.title: Definition of hamartoma
questions.question: Which is the correct definition of a hamartoma?

options.A: Disorganised native tissue growing in its own normal site
options.B: Normal tissue growing in an abnormal site
options.C: A tumor derived from totipotent cells, containing tissue from more than one germ layer
options.D: A benign tumor of glandular epithelium

explanations.A: Correct. A hamartoma is a disorganised, tumour-like overgrowth of tissue elements native to the site it grows in — normal cell types, at their normal site, but in an abnormal arrangement and proportion. Normal tissue in an abnormal site is the definition of choristoma instead, the direct opposite pairing.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes a choristoma, not a hamartoma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes a teratoma, a different developmental tumour entirely.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This describes an adenoma, a benign glandular epithelial tumour, not a hamartoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that a hamartoma is disorganised tissue at its normal site, not normal tissue at an abnormal site.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Hamartoma is normal tissue in abnormal site", p399

questions.title: Definition of metaplasia
questions.question: Which is the correct definition of metaplasia?

options.A: Replacement of one differentiated tissue type by another differentiated tissue type
options.B: Disordered growth within one tissue type, with loss of cell uniformity and architectural orientation
options.C: Irreversible, autonomous proliferation of a new clone of cells
options.D: An increase in cell size without an increase in cell number

explanations.A: Correct. Metaplasia is the replacement of one differentiated tissue type by another differentiated tissue type, usually a reversible adaptive response to chronic irritation. Loss of cell uniformity and architectural orientation within one tissue type is the definition of dysplasia instead, a common exam swap.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This describes dysplasia's definition, not metaplasia's.
explanations.C: Incorrect. This describes neoplasia, an irreversible autonomous process, distinct from metaplasia, which remains a reversible adaptive change.
explanations.D: Incorrect. An increase in cell size without increased number describes hypertrophy, not metaplasia.

questions.learning_objective: State that metaplasia is tissue-type replacement, not disordered growth within one tissue type.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Metaplasia is disorder of cell growth...loss in uniformity", p399

questions.title: Is carcinoma benign or malignant
questions.question: Which correctly defines a carcinoma?

options.A: A malignant tumor of epithelial cell origin
options.B: A benign tumor of epithelial cell origin
options.C: A malignant tumor of mesenchymal (connective-tissue) origin
options.D: A benign tumor of mesenchymal (connective-tissue) origin

explanations.A: Correct. A carcinoma is, by definition, a malignant neoplasm of epithelial cell origin. Papillomas and adenomas are the benign counterparts of epithelial-origin tumours; sarcomas are the malignant mesenchymal-origin counterparts.
explanations.B: Incorrect. "Benign" epithelial tumours are papillomas or adenomas, not carcinomas.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin is a sarcoma, not a carcinoma.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A benign tumour of mesenchymal origin (e.g. a fibroma or leiomyoma) is neither malignant nor epithelial, so it is not a carcinoma.

questions.learning_objective: State that carcinoma is a malignant, not benign, epithelial-origin tumour.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Carcinoma is a benign epithelial tumor", p399

questions.title: Growth rate: benign versus malignant
questions.question: Which is generally true of tumour growth rate?

options.A: Malignant tumors generally grow rapidly; benign tumors generally grow slowly
options.B: Benign tumors generally grow rapidly; malignant tumors generally grow slowly
options.C: Both grow at similar average rates
options.D: Growth rate does not correlate with malignancy at all

explanations.A: Correct. As a general rule, malignant tumours grow rapidly, reflecting their higher mitotic rate and loss of normal growth control, while benign tumours grow slowly over months to years. Exceptions exist on both sides, but the exam-tested default direction is malignant = fast, benign = slow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This statement reverses the standard teaching.
explanations.C: Incorrect. On average the two categories differ substantially in typical growth rate, not similarly.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Growth rate is one of the classic features used to help distinguish benign from malignant tumours, so it does correlate, as a general tendency.

questions.learning_objective: State that malignant tumours generally grow rapidly and benign tumours generally grow slowly.
questions.module_subject: O6U-IPA-107 > General Pathology > Neoplasia

field_notes.keySource: printed inline "( false )" against "Most benign tumors grow rapidly whereas most malignant tumors grow slowly", p399

questions.title: Definition of cellular anaplasia
questions.question: Which correctly defines cellular anaplasia?

options.A: Changes in cellular morphology and loss of polarity
options.D: Reduction in cell size without cell loss

explanations.A: Correct. Anaplasia — cellular and nuclear pleomorphism, loss of polarity, and abnormal mitoses — grades how far a malignant tumour's cells have drifted from the normal appearance and arrangement of their tissue of origin. Worse differentiation means faster growth and more anaplasia, not less, since anaplasia and differentiation move in opposite directions.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Increased extracellular matrix deposition describes fibrosis, not anaplasia.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Programmed cell death without inflammation describes apoptosis, not anaplasia.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reduction in cell size without cell loss describes atrophy, not anaplasia.

questions.learning_objective: Define cellular anaplasia as changes in cellular morphology and loss of polarity.
